passage: Looking back, the evening Vishal came home with the offer letter is when our budget stopped feeling sacred. The new job suited Vishal better, but the salary was lower, and the sheet we had drawn up so proudly no longer added up. My first instinct was to defend it. We had agreed on it, after all. Then I saw the red at the bottom of the column and asked myself what an agreement is for. On Sunday we sat with tea and the laptop and called it a review meeting. We dropped the weekend eating-out line and the streaming and gadget line, and each of us changed our monthly share to match what we actually earn. Nothing felt like a defeat. The sheet is ours, and it can change when we do. - Amandeep

Money-skills coach's note — young couples group, Thane. Written by Charu.

I've worked with Harsha and her husband, Sameer, since last spring, when they set up their household rules: fixed contributions to a joint account, set amounts for eating out, clothes, gadgets and savings.
In September Harsha left her corporate job to join a small non-profit. Her salary dropped by a lot. Many couples try to carry on as before and quietly run short. These two didn't.
They asked for a separate session just for this. They brought their sheet and went through each line aloud. Harsha said, "The old rules were written for two corporate salaries." They cut eating out and gadgets for now, and changed the contributions so Sameer puts in a larger share until things change again.
Sameer said, "It's our agreement. We can edit it."
My next step: I've marked a follow-up session in six months.

qa.q: When did Harsha leave her corporate job?
How might Harsha have felt saying the old rules were written for two corporate salaries?
qa.a: She may have felt a little anxious about the drop in income but relieved to name it openly so they could adjust together.

qa.q: What else could Harsha and Sameer do if their income changes again?
qa.a: They could hold another special meeting, look at each category together, and if unsure of options, speak to a qualified adviser.

qa.q: How does the change look from Sameer's side?
qa.a: Sameer takes on a larger share for now and sees the rules as a shared agreement they can edit, not a law he must defend.

grounding: It shows a couple holding a special meeting after one partner's income drops, cutting two categories and adjusting contributions as a working agreement.

Thursday night

Akash's last day at the bank was Friday. He starts at the start-up on Monday: work he actually loves, and a lot less pay.
We could have ignored it and just hoped. But we sat down tonight with our money sheet, the one we wrote a year ago with all our rules on it. Fixed amounts into the joint account, amounts for food delivery, shopping, weekends away.
Akash said, "These rules belong to a different month." He's right.
We decided: no weekends away till Diwali, and food delivery down to once a week. And I'll put in a bigger share to the joint account for now, since I'm earning more. It felt strange writing that, but also fair.
We changed the date at the top of the sheet. Version two.
I thought it would be a fight. It was just two people adjusting a plan.
— Himani

qa.q: When does Akash start at the start-up?
How did Himani feel about the meeting, compared with what Himani expected?
qa.a: Himani expected a fight but felt relieved and calm, since it was just two people adjusting a plan.

qa.q: What else could Himani and Akash add to their new version?
qa.a: They could set a date to revisit the rules again, so the sheet keeps pace with any further change.

qa.q: How might Akash see the changes to the rules?
qa.a: Akash probably feels supported and less guilty about the pay cut, since Himani treats it as a shared adjustment rather than a problem he caused.

grounding: It shows a couple meeting after one partner's income drops, cutting two categories and changing contributions, treating their rules as a working agreement.
